On 4 May 2019 The Financial Times (FT) reported that Huawei is planning to build a "400-person chip research and development factory" outside Cambridge. Planned to be operational by 2021, the factory will include an R&D centre and will be built on a 550-acre site reportedly purchased by Huawei in 2018 for 37.5 million pounds. A Huawei spokesperson quoted in this FT article cited Huawei's long-term collaboration with Cambridge University which includes a 5-year 25 million pound research partnership with BT which launched a joint research group at the University of Cambridge. In 2017 Serbia's Ministry of Interior and Huawei signed a 'strategic agreement' to implement a 'Safe City' solution. Part 1 of this solution included the deployment of 100 surveillance cameras, a re-modelled command and control centre in Belgrade, facial & license plate recognition, intelligence analysis systems, behaviour analysis capabilities and a data centre. Huawei's website states: 'Together with Huawei, [Serbia's] Ministry of Interior will develop a comprehensive Safe City solution that covers the city of Belgrade, and eventually the entire country, through critical communications, converged command centers, and intelligent surveillance.' In 2018 Serbia's Finance Minister and Huawei signed an agreement for the 'procurement of equipment, work and services for the realisation of a capital transportation surveillance.’ The system is planned to include 1000 cameras in 800 locations across Belgrade. 

Many in Serbia have raised concerns with they system, including Serbia’s former commissioner for personal data protection. He said ‘the system can be used to trail political opponents, monitor regime critics at any moment, which is completely against the law.’ Groups opposed to the President say ‘say police are leaking video of protests to pro-government media, which publish the images, along with the identities of participants.’ 

Nenad Popovic, Serbian minister in charge of innovation and technological development, said in October 2019 that Huawei is set to present the functioning of 5G technology with Telekom, a Serbian telecom public enterprise.

Huawei provides services and equipment - including surveillance cameras, data storage systems & a portable rapid deployment system - to the Ecuadorian Government's public security system known as "ECU 911". Considered a Belt and Road project and initially funded by a USD 240 million Chinese state loan in 2012, the system is used by the country's military, police and fire brigade. Chinese defence SOE China National Electronics Import and Export Corporation (CEIEC) was contracted to construct the system, and later to provide services in support of the centre's operations. This includes the provision of CEIEC engineers & technicians who work in the system's lab and command centres. The system reportedly includes facial recognition technologies and 16 national, regional and provincial command and control centres, as well as a data laboratory and research partnerships. In 2017 the Chinese embassy donated a further USD 15 million of equipment including license plate recognition cameras and servers. Chinese state media has reported that the new system has resulted in a 11.8% drop in Ecuador's crime rate and highlighted the system's ability to respond rapidly in disaster relief situations. There have been reports in the Ecuadorian media of corruption, missing money and opaque deals linked to the system. Before the system launched in 2016 Ecuadorian delegations travelled to China to learn about China's security structures and about how similar centres operate. The model, which has resulted in a huge increase in installed surveillance cameras in Ecuador, is reportedly being rolled out in other countries including Peru, Zimbabwe and Cambodia. In 2017 ECU 911 won best public security project in Latin America. Watch this CEIEC promotional video about ECU 911

In response to concerns about backdoors and other security risks that may be associated with Huawei equipment, the Huawei Cyber Security Evaluation Centre was established in the UK in 2010. This reflects a different approach towards Huawei technology than that taken in Australia, which has opted to ban Huawei and other high-risk vendors from critical infrastructure projects. Some of the centre’s staff, including its managing director, joined directly from Huawei.

Security risks were first identified in the Centre Oversight Board’s 2018 annual report, which highlighted that “technical issues have been identified in Huawei engineering processes.” Further, the oversight board stated in the 2018 report that it could provide “only limited assurance that all risks to UK national security from Huawei’s involvement in the UK’s critical networks have been sufficiently mitigated.”

The oversight board’s March 2019 annual report found these security issues with Huawei products to be ongoing, and continued to provide “only limited assurance that the long-term security risks can be managed in the Huawei equipment currently deployed in the UK.“

Despite these concerns, the 2019 annual report stated: “the Oversight Board has not yet seen anything to give it confidence in Huawei’s capacity to successfully complete the elements of its transformation programme that it has proposed as a means of addressing these underlying defects.”

The Djibouti Data Center (DDC) is an important piece of infrastructure in China's pan-Africa expansion as part of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). It offers cable head access to Djibouti Telecom's Djibouti landing station (located only metres away) that has access to over half a dozen submarine cables including AAE1 (Asia-Africa-Europe), SMW3 (South East Asia - Middle East - Western Europe), SMW5, as well as China's own Pakistan East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE) cable project. Furthermore DDC houses the Djibouti Internet Exchange (DjIX).

The agreement between China Mobile International and Djibouti Data Center extends beyond just the use of rack space in its COLO, probably for the use of DjIX to interconnect networks with other operators and extend their CDN (content delivery network), but also cable head access to the landing station and its available undersea cables.

According to DDC's CEO, China Unicom, has a relationship with the the DDC. It is not clear whether this link is indirect, via the PEACE cable project, via its investment in Hong Kong telco, PCCW which has annouced its use of the DDC for colocation and cable access, or a direct link. It is likely there is a direct connection as DDC provides cross connect services which would allow China Unicom to reduce costs and connect to foreign partner networks that are also using the DDC. Additionally with DDC's cable head access, this would allow China Unicom to connect into PEACE cable, SEAMEW-5 and AAE-1 undersea cables.

In June 2016, China Unicom led the creation of China–ASEAN Information Harbor Co. Ltd (中国—东盟信息港股份有限公司, 中国东信)—a State Council-approved state-owned company of which it is the majority shareholder (45%). In 2017, that company and Tropic Science Co. Ltd, using financing from the China Construction Bank, were the key investors behind the PEACE cable project (丝路国际海缆网络系统项目, PEACE项目). PEACE (Pakistan – East Africa Connecting Europe) is part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. It is an undersea cable expected to be ready for service in the first quarter of 2020. Including the cross-border connection between China and Pakistan, after its completion the cable will be the shortest length and latency route connecting China with Africa and Europe.

This will not only provide China with high-speed access to Africa, but also link the country’s assets in Africa back to China. It will land in Djibouti, where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has a naval base. The PEACE cable also lands in Gwadar, Pakistan, where it will connect with the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Gwadar has long been speculated as a likely site for a PLA Navy and Air base. It has been reported the construction of this cable will also improve the quality of local network services in Somalia and the Seychelles.

It’s unclear what happened in the months between the start of the project and October 2018, when the laying of the cable started, but ownership of the project had shifted from state-owned China–ASEAN Information Harbor and Tropical Science to PEACE Cable International Network Co. Ltd, a subsidiary of Hengtong Group. The cable was manufactured by Hengtong Group’s subsidiary, Hengtong Marine, and Huawei Marine provided the transmission platform. By November 2018, it was stated that the 12,000-kilometre PEACE cable system was ‘privately owned by Hengtong Group’ (Capacity magazine, page 56).

In 2014 Huawei gave the Ugandan government 20 surveillance cameras valued at US$750,000. In 2015 Huawei ‘signed a deal to become the Ugandan government’s sole information-communications partner.’ 

According to the Wall Street Journal, in May 2018 Uganda and Huawei signed a US$126 million deal for a ‘safe-cities’ project. Uganda paid $16.3 million up front and used a $104 million Standard Chartered Bank loan. According to the Financial Times, on 21 August 2019 Ugandan police confirmed that Huawei was rolling out a Safe City initiative in Uganda in response to the WSJ investigation. The system includes facial recognition and artificial intelligence software and closed-circuit television cameras nationwide.

On 15 August 2019, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huawei technicians helped intelligence officials in Uganda to spy on their political opponents, ‘including intercepting their encrypted communications and social media, and using cell data to track their whereabouts.’ According to the Wall Street Journal investigation Huawei engineers helped Ugandan intelligence officers penetrate the communications of a key political opponent. This reportedly led to the arrest of the politician and some of his supporters. Uganda’s government confirmed that Huawei was proving technical support to their intelligence community and police, but declined to comment on the spying allegations. Huawei denied the allegations. 

According to the WSJ investigation President Museveni directed his then-police chief to approach the CCP for assistance with digital surveillance in 2017, in response to protests. In September 2017. Senior Ugandan security officials went to Algiers to study their video surveillance system, at the advice of Huawei. Also in 2017, Ugandan police officers received technical training in Beijing.Huawei technicians were seconded to train local staff on how to use Huawei technology for Uganda’s first cyber unit, opened in November 2018. 

Reportedly, the first phase of the project would connect 83 police stations in the capital. There are plans to expand it to another 271 police stations. Huawe has also assisted in the construction of 11 monitoring systems and a forthcoming $30 mullion hub. This hub is to be linked to 5,000 of the company’s cameras equipped with facial recognition technology.

All the above information is from the Wall Street Journal investigation.

In July 2018 representatives from Huawei met with the Governor of the province of Mendoza to discuss ‘public safety’ technology. Access Now and other civil society organisations working in Argentina sent a letter to the Mendoza government outlining their concerns surrounding the potential of these technologies to violate human rights. They called on Mendoza’s government not to acquire Huawei’s smart city technologies until a public debate takes place including a process around securing privacy rights.

In April 2019, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. announced that it is working with Tencent Honor of Kings, Tencent AI Lab, and Vivo on applying AI to gaming experiences.

In October 2018, Tencent, Medopad, and the Parkinson's Centre of Excellence at King's College Hospital in London teamed up to apply AI in diagnosing Parkinson’s disease. According to Dr. Wei Fan, head of Tencent’s Medical AI Lab, “Tencent provides the AI technology and capabilities for the video analysis of Parkinson’s disease motor function which will be used in Medopad’s mobile application.”  The Financial Times reported in May 2019 that Tencent has started a clinical trial of the program in London.

In September 2019, Amazon announced that it is partnering with several tech companies, including Tencent, on establishing the Voice Interoperability Initiative, a project that is committed to “making products with voice control capabilities more flexible, allowing users to wake up the devices with different wake-up commands and to choose among multiple different voice services.” The WeChat AI team of Tencent will contribute its smart voice assistant solutions and its consumer experience data to fuel Ai algorithms.

In April 2018, Tencent and Babylon Health, a British digital health start-up, reached a strategic cooperation agreement. According to Financial Times, Tencent offered its WeChat platform and Babylon offered its app that uses AI to assess illness.

In November 2018, Alibaba Cloud and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University signed a MOU on cooperation on Artificial Intelligence research, especially in promoting the development of smart cities and smart medical work. Since 2016, the university has been cooperating closely with Alibaba Group in many areas. In March 2018, they launched a “Fashion AI Database,” combining the fashion industry and AI to enhance the personalized shopping experience.

In January 2019, Alibaba and Intel jointly launched a new artificial intelligence sports player tracking technology. The technology uses multiple cameras and utilizes deep learning algorithms to render athletes into 3D form during training or competition. This model allows the instructor to observe complex real-time biomechanical data to analyze player performance and introduce new training enhancements.
In September 2019, Alibaba Cloud and Facebook announced their joint partnership. Facebook's open source deep learning framework PyTorch will station in the Alibaba Cloud machine learning platform.
In May 2019, Alibaba and L’oreal cooperate in developing Effaclar Spotscan, a AI acne analysis application. The service is available on Tmall and Taobao mobile phones applications in June 2019.

Currently, they have worked together in the field of autopilot.

In March 2019, BGI and Natera, a genetic testing company based in California, United States, signed a 10-year-long cooperation agreement that worth $US 50 million on commercializing Natera's Signatera Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) test in China and conduct reproductive health testing in designated markets. All of these tests would be using sequencing technology and instruments of BGI.

In June 2019, MGI Tech Co., Ltd, a subsidiary of BGI, collaborates in microbiome research with the Centre for Translational Microbiome Research (CTMR) at Karolinska Institutet. According to the MGI’s statement, the collaboration will “use MGI’s DNBSEQTM technology to generate high quality shotgun metagenomics data from one of the largest microbiome biobanks.” In September 2019, Wan Gang, the Vice Chairman of the CPPCC and the Chairman of the China Association for Science and Technology, visited Karolinska Institute, where MGI provides a sequencing platform. He said to MGI staff that “MGI should not only ‘build’ good machines, but also ‘use’ good machines, which is to let the world's top institutions and experts use the equipment made by MGI!”
